title: Checkpoint: How Stories Work
objective: After this level you can take any story apart into its plot, conflict, characters, narrator and theme.
summary: Forster: a story is events in time order; a plot adds cause ("of grief"). The toolkit got its names from 1863 to 1961. Try it on Aesop's fox.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: a king, a queen and a whole toolkit.
cards.body: Two short sentences from E. M. Forster hold the difference between a story and a plot. Then, one old fable, taken apart with every tool from this chapter.

cards.headline: When the tools got their names

events.label: Freytag draws drama as a pyramid
Forster sorts characters into flat and round

cards.headline: The king died, and then...
cards.body: Forster: "The king died and then the queen died" is a story, events in their time sequence. "The king died, and then the queen died of grief" is a plot: the emphasis falls on causality. Two words, "of grief", turn a list into a reason. Every tool in this chapter asks the same question underneath: why?

cards.headline: Take apart a fable
cards.body: Try it on Level 2's fox. Plot: he jumps again and again for grapes he can't reach, then walks off calling them sour. Conflict: what he wants, and what stands in the way. Theme: here the fable states it outright as its moral, "There are many who pretend to despise and belittle that which is beyond their reach."

mascot.line: Five questions open any story: what happens, what's in the way, who changes, who's telling it, and what it means.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How to take a story apart into its plot, conflict, characters, narrator and theme.
What separates a story from a plot, and a flat character from a round one.
Which clues warn you that a narrator can't be trusted.
How genre, symbols and the hero's journey shape what readers expect.

questions.prompt: How does Forster turn "The king died and then the queen died" from a story into a plot?

options.label: By adding a cause: the queen died of grief
By swapping the order of the deaths
options.rationale: Order alone is still a story.

options.label: By adding a third royal death
options.rationale: More events don't make a plot; causes do.

options.label: By telling it in first person
options.rationale: That's a change of point of view, not plot.

questions.explanation: A plot puts the emphasis on causality: "The king died, and then the queen died of grief."

questions.prompt: Chapter recap: which of these story tools got its name first?
questions.explanation: Freytag drew his pyramid in 1863, long before Forster (1927), Campbell (1949) and Booth (1961).

questions.prompt: From Level 24: which point of view gives a panoramic view of the characters' actions and inner feelings?

options.label: First person
options.rationale: That gives one narrator's mind only.

questions.explanation: Omniscient narration gives a panoramic view of the actions and inner feelings of the characters.

questions.prompt: From Level 26: how should you state a story's theme?

options.label: As a single word, like "death"
options.rationale: That's the subject, not yet the theme.

options.label: As one sentence with a subject and a verb
As a list of the main events
options.rationale: A theme is not a summary.

options.label: As the name of the narrator

questions.explanation: Take the topic, add an assertion, and write the theme as one sentence with a subject and a verb.

questions.prompt: From Level 23: Forster's test for a round character is whether it can do what?

options.label: Tell the story in first person
Surprise the reader in a convincing way
State the moral at the end
options.rationale: Morals belong to fables, not to the round-character test.

questions.explanation: Forster: "The test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way."
